newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-AUSTRALIA LOSE ELLIOTT BUT TIGHTEN GRIP.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-AUSTRALIA LOSE ELLIOTT BUT TIGHTEN GRIP.

text.p: Australia captain Mark Taylor set West Indies a target of 340 runs to win the second test on a day of despair for fellow opener Matthew Elliott on Monday.

West Indies openers Sherwin Campbell and Robert Samuels survived 12 tense overs late in the day to steer the tourists to 27 for no wicket at close of play on the fourth day at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

With their hopes of winning all but extinguished because of the slowness of the wicket, West Indies face the more realistic task of batting through a minimum of 90 overs on the fifth and final day to earn a draw.
Although few batsmen have been troubled by the wicket in terms of survival, all have struggled to score runs freely.
Elliott was denied a likely maiden test century when he was forced to retire hurt on 78 because of a knee injury after a painful collision with team-mate Mark Waugh.
Elliott is set to undergo surgery on Wednesday to repair cartilage damage and could be out of action for three weeks, an Australian Cricket Board spokesman said.
"I did not feel any pain at the moment of impact but I did as soon as I landed," Elliott said in a statement. "I can't believe this has happened."
Elliott and Waugh collided as they sprinted between the wickets in search of a second run with the total on 143 for two just before lunch.

Although both batsmen were knocked to the ground, Elliott managed to dive back to the safety of his crease, foiling West Indies' attempt to run him out. But he was unable to carry on batting after lengthy treatment.
It was cruel luck for Elliott, who made his test debut in the first test in Brisbane as a replacement for out-of-form opener Michael Slater.

Waugh made amends for his involvement in the incident by hitting a patient 67 as Australia painstakingly advanced to 312 for four in their second innings before Taylor declared the innings 40 minutes before the scheduled close.
West Indies endured a dismal day in the field after Australia resumed on 77 for two, an overall lead of 104 runs.

Whatever faint hopes West Indies held of winning the match were dispelled by Australia's middle order batsmen, who applied themselves with grim determination to the task of grinding out runs on a difficult, slow wicket.
West Indies' fielding, mediocre to begin with, deteriorated badly under the pressure. Several catches were spilled and the Australian batsmen benefited further from countless misfields.
Australia's slow progress frustrated the tourists and provided scant entertainment for a paltry crowd of little more than 11,000.
Australia, who won the first test by 123 runs, scored 331 in their first innings in Sydney before dismissing West Indies for 304.
